title: Improper Integrals and Probability Densities
objectives: Define improper integrals over infinite intervals and evaluate convergent cases by limits
Apply the $p$-test to decide convergence of $\int_1^\infty x^{-p}\,dx$
Verify the defining properties of a probability density and compute probabilities as integrals
Derive tail probabilities and means for the exponential distribution
Work a heavy-tail-flavoured loss density end to end: total mass, tail probability and mean
motivation: Unbounded waiting times and loss models often need integrals over infinite domains. Improper integration defines these by limits and distinguishes finite total probability from finite moments. Not every loss model is unbounded, not every risk measure is an improper integral, and a valid density can still have infinite mean or variance. These distinctions matter before trusting a numerical risk report.

blocks.text: Infinity as a limit, not a number

blocks.md: An integral over an infinite interval is *defined* by cutting it back to a finite endpoint $b$, integrating, and then sending $b \to \infty$ - Lesson 1's limit machinery again, now applied to areas:

blocks.caption: Definition of an improper integral over $[1, \infty)$

blocks.md: If the limit exists (finite), the integral **converges**; otherwise it **diverges**. The most important comparison pair shows how brutally sensitive convergence is to decay rate:

blocks.title: Worked derivation: the $p$-test pair
items: $\displaystyle\int_1^b \frac{dx}{x} = \ln b - \ln 1 = \ln b$; as $b \to \infty$ this grows without bound. Diverges.
Intuition: $1/x^2$ decays *fast enough* that each extra slab adds a shrinking amount whose sum settles; $1/x$ shrinks too slowly, like a harmonic series, and the accumulation never stops.

Contrast with the other improper type: an unbounded *integrand* near a point, e.g. $\int_0^1 \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x}} = [2\sqrt{x}]_0^1 = 2$ converges despite the blow-up at $0$ - area can be finite even where the function spikes.

blocks.md: A continuous random variable $X$ is described by a **probability density** $f(x)$ with two defining properties: $f(x) \ge 0$ everywhere, and $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx = 1$ - the *whole* real line's area is one full unit of certainty, typically an improper integral. Probabilities are areas over ranges: $P(a \le X \le b) = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx$. Since single points have zero width, $P(X = x) = 0$ - only *ranges* carry probability. Expectations integrate value-weighted density: $\mathbb{E}[X] = \int x f(x)\,dx$, itself improper whenever the support is unbounded.

blocks.title: Worked derivation: the exponential distribution
items: For constant hazard lambda>0, f(x)=lambda*exp(-lambda*x) for x>=0 and zero otherwise. Survival exp(-lambda*t) is stated for t>=0; for t<0 it is 1.
Total mass: $\int_0^\infty \lambda e^{-\lambda x}dx = \left[-e^{-\lambda x}\right]_0^\infty = 0 - (-1) = 1$. Verified, a proper density.
Tail probability: $P(X > t) = \int_t^\infty \lambda e^{-\lambda x}dx = e^{-\lambda t}$ - the survival function.
For $\lambda = 0.1$ per year (mean waiting time $1/\lambda = 10$ years): $P(X > 10) = e^{-1} \approx 0.3679$, $P(X > 20) = e^{-2} \approx 0.1353$.

Mean: $\mathbb{E}[X] = \int_0^\infty x\,\lambda e^{-\lambda x}dx$ - integration by parts (Lesson 8) gives $\left[-xe^{-\lambda x}\right]_0^\infty + \int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda x}dx = 0 + \frac{1}{\lambda} = \frac{1}{\lambda}$. With $\lambda = 0.1$: mean $= 10$ years, consistent.

blocks.code:
import math
lam = 0.1
for t in [5, 10, 20]:
    print(round(math.exp(-lam * t), 4))
blocks.caption: For lambda=0.1, survival at 5,10,20 years is 0.6065,0.3679,0.1353. Halving the hazard takes the square root of a fixed-time survival probability, rather than doubling it.

blocks.md: Two-sided improper integrals require each one-sided integral to converge separately. An odd function may have zero symmetric principal value even when its ordinary improper integral diverges. Likewise, a finite expectation of a signed variable requires integrability of the absolute value; canceling divergent positive and negative parts is not a mean. Nonnegative losses can have a well-defined extended expectation of positive infinity. For example, an integrable probability density need not have an integrable x-weighted density. Check total mass and each moment separately.

blocks.title: Does the tail pay its way? Three integrals, three verdicts
items: $\int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x^2}\,dx = \left[-\frac{1}{x}\right]_1^\infty = 0 - (-1) = 1$. Converges. Power $p > 1$ always does, the tail area is finite.

$\int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x}\,dx = \left[\ln x\right]_1^\infty = \infty$. Diverges, *logarithmically slowly*. This is the trap: numerically, partial sums grow so slowly that a finite experiment will convince you it converges. It does not.

$\int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x^{p}}\,dx$ converges iff $p > 1$; $\int_0^1 \frac{1}{x^{p}}\,dx$ converges iff $p < 1$. Same function family, opposite verdicts at opposite ends, the infinite side and the singular side test different behaviour.

blocks.md: Keep density and survival exponents separate. If a nonnegative loss density behaves as c*x^(-p) in the far tail, its tail mass is finite only for p>1, its mean is finite only for p>2, and its second moment is finite only for p>3. More generally its k-th positive moment is finite only for p>k+1 under this power-law asymptotic. A survival tail behaving as x^(-alpha) instead has alpha=p-1; its positive k-th moment requires k<alpha. Always state which exponent is being quoted.

blocks.title: A valid density can have infinite variance
blocks.md: For f(x)=2/(1+x)^3 on x>=0, the survival tail is(1+x)^(-2). It has finite mean 1 but infinite second moment, since x^2*f(x) behaves as 2/x. Thus variance is infinite. A survival index 3 would instead give a finite second moment; saying only index 3 without defining density or survival exponent is ambiguous. Finite samples still return finite sample variances, but that does not establish a finite population variance or imply every sample estimate must understate every chosen tail-risk measure.

blocks.caption: On[0,20] the exponential density integrates to 1-exp(-2), about 0.864665. The remaining exp(-2), about 13.53%, lies beyond 20; a finite cutoff is not the whole probability mass.

blocks.text: The normal density and heavy tails

blocks.md: For the standard normal density phi(x)=exp(-x^2/2)/sqrt(2*pi), Phi(1) is approximately 0.841345: that is the mass below+1, not the mass within one standard deviation. The central probability P(-1<=Z<=1)=Phi(1)-Phi(-1) is approximately 0.682689. The normal density decays faster than any inverse power and all polynomial moments are finite. Numerical quadrature or specialised normal-CDF routines can compute probabilities without an elementary antiderivative. Power-law models need separate checks for normalisation and moments, not just a comparison of visual tail thickness.

blocks.title: A complete loss model, by hand
blocks.md: For loss density f(x)=2/(1+x)^3 on x>=0 and zero otherwise, the antiderivative is-(1+x)^(-2). Total mass is 1, survival is(1+t)^(-2) for t>=0, and P(X>1)=1/4. Substitution u=1+x gives mean integral of 2u^(-2)-2u^(-3) over[1,infinity), equal to 2-1=1. The second moment diverges. These quantities describe selected aspects of the model, not an entire risk profile; specify thresholds, units and the required risk measure.

guidedExercise.prompt: An exponential model uses hazard $\lambda = 0.25$ per year. (a) Verify the density integrates to 1. (b) Compute $P(X \le 4)$ and $P(X > 4)$. (c) State $\mathbb{E}[X]$ and check it against the survival probabilities.
hints: Antiderivative of $\lambda e^{-\lambda x}$ is $-e^{-\lambda x}$.
$\mathbb{E}[X] = 1/\lambda$ for the exponential, compare $\lambda = 0.25$ with the Lesson 8 by-parts result.
Evaluate finite-endpoint integrals first, then take limits; compare density, survival and moment exponents separately.
guidedExercise.solution: (a) $\int_0^\infty 0.25e^{-0.25x}dx = \left[-e^{-0.25x}\right]_0^\infty = 0 - (-1) = \mathbf{1}$. (b) $P(X > 4) = e^{-0.25 \times 4} = e^{-1} = 0.3679$, so $P(X \le 4) = 1 - 0.3679 = \mathbf{0.6321}$. (c) $\mathbb{E}[X] = 1/\lambda = \mathbf{4}$ years. The median is ln(2)/0.25, approximately 2.772589 years, not 4. At the mean 4 years the CDF is 1-exp(-1), about 0.632121, which is consistent with this right-skewed distribution.
guidedExercise.successCheck: Mass 1; survival at 4 is exp(-1), CDF 1-exp(-1), mean 4 years; median about 2.772589.

independentExercise.prompt: Loss severity has density $f(x) = \dfrac{2}{(1+x)^3}$ for $x \ge 0$. (a) Verify $\int_0^\infty f = 1$. (b) Compute $P(X > 1)$. (c) Compute $\mathbb{E}[X]$ using the substitution $u = 1 + x$. (d) Compare the tail decay with the exponential $\lambda = 1$ model's $e^{-t}$ - which model produces bigger extreme losses?
hints: After substituting $u = 1+x$, split $2(u-1)u^{-3}$ into two standard $p$-integrals.
Evaluate finite-endpoint integrals first, then take limits; compare density, survival and moment exponents separately.
independentExercise.solution: (a) $\int_0^\infty 2(1+x)^{-3}dx = \left[-(1+x)^{-2}\right]_0^\infty = 1$. (b) $P(X>1) = \left[-(1+x)^{-2}\right]_1^\infty = 1/4 = \mathbf{0.25}$. (c) $\mathbb{E}[X] = \int_1^\infty 2(u-1)u^{-3}du = \int_1^\infty (2u^{-2} - 2u^{-3})du = [2 \cdot 1 - 2 \cdot \tfrac{1}{2}] = \mathbf{1}$. (d) The loss survival is(1+t)^(-2), whereas the exponential survival is exp(-t). For sufficiently large t the power-law survival is larger. At t=1 it is 0.25, which is smaller than exp(-1), so do not claim it dominates at every threshold. Compare survival tails, not the density exponent 3 with an exceedance probability exponent. The two distributions have the same mean 1 but different far-tail and second-moment behaviour.
independentExercise.successCheck: Mass 1, tail at 1=1/4, mean 1; survival(1+t)^(-2) is eventually heavier than exp(-t), not at every threshold.

commonMistakes: Writing $\int_1^\infty \frac{dx}{x} = \ln(\infty)$ as if it were a value, it diverges; say so explicitly.
Assuming any positive integrable-looking density is valid, always check the total mass is exactly 1.
Computing $P(X = x)$ for a continuous variable, it is 0; only intervals have probability.
Mixing the mean formula for discrete variables ($\sum$) with the continuous one ($\int x f(x)dx$).
realWorldApplication: Improper integrals help evaluate unbounded waiting-time and loss models. Bounded-support probabilities may use proper integrals, and discrete models use sums. Exponential arrivals require particular modelling assumptions; they are not a universal queueing law.
quantFinanceApplication: Constant positive hazard gives exponential survival in a simple credit model. VaR is a quantile, found from a CDF or survival equation; it is not itself an expected-loss integral. Expected shortfall is a conditional-tail average under appropriate definitions and may be infinite even when a quantile is finite.
summary: Improper integrals are limits: $\int_1^\infty f = \lim_{b\to\infty}\int_1^b f$; finite limit = converge, else diverge.
A density satisfies $f \ge 0$ and $\int f = 1$; probabilities are range integrals and $P(X = x) = 0$.
For constant lambda>0 and t>=0, exponential survival is exp(-lambda*t) and mean1/lambda. At lambda=0.1 per year, survival past10 years is about0.367879 and mean10 years.
For density decay x^(-p), normalisation requires p>1, a finite mean p>2 and finite second moment p>3. A survival exponent alpha=p-1 uses different thresholds; specify the convention.

quiz.explanation: By the $p$-test, $\int_1^\infty x^{-p}dx$ converges only for $p > 1$; $1/x$ has $p = 1$ and accumulates to $\ln b \to \infty$. The others converge ($1$ and $1/2$, and $2$ respectively).

quiz.prompt: A default time follows an exponential model with hazard $\lambda = 0.1$ per year. What is $P(\text{survival past } t = 10)$, i.e. $P(X > 10)$? (4 decimal places)
quiz.explanation: With constant positive hazard 0.1 per year and t=10 years, survival is exp(-0.1*10)=exp(-1), approximately 0.367879. The complementary probability of default by 10 years is about 0.632121.

quiz.prompt: For the exponential model with $\lambda = 0.25$, what is $\mathbb{E}[X]$ in years?
quiz.explanation: The mean of an exponential is $1/\lambda = 4$ years, derived via integration by parts on $\int_0^\infty x\,\lambda e^{-\lambda x}dx$.

quiz.prompt: What does this Python code print?
quiz.code:
import math
lam = 0.1
for t in [5, 10, 20]:
    print(round(math.exp(-lam * t), 4))
quiz.explanation: Exponential survival probabilities $e^{-0.1t}$: halving the mean wait (hazard doubling) squares the tail probability.

quiz.prompt: Which set of properties makes $f$ a valid probability density on $[0, \infty)$?
options: $\int_0^\infty f(x)\,dx = 1$ is sufficient on its own
quiz.explanation: Non-negativity plus total mass 1 are exactly the two axioms; the maximum is irrelevant (densities can exceed 1 on narrow ranges), and non-negativity cannot be dropped since negative area would corrupt probabilities.

quiz.prompt: If a nonnegative loss density has tail f(x) proportional to x^(-p), what p thresholds give finite tail mass and finite mean? Distinguish the density exponent from the survival exponent.
quiz.modelAnswer: For a power-law density tail, integrable tail mass needs p>1, but a finite mean needs p>2 because x*f(x) behaves as x^(1-p). The survival tail exponent is alpha=p-1, so finite mean requires alpha>1. A valid heavy-tail density can have infinite mean.
quiz.explanation: Normalisation integrates f itself, whereas the mean integrates x*f. Their p-test thresholds differ by 1. A survival exponent is one less than the density exponent in this power-law setting; confusing them gives incorrect moment claims.

quiz.prompt: Evaluate the convergent improper integral of x^(-2) from 1 to infinity by a finite-endpoint limit. What is its value?
quiz.explanation: For finite b>1, the integral is[-1/x]_1^b=1-1/b. Taking b to infinity gives 1, a finite limit. Infinity is used as a limit, not substituted as an ordinary endpoint number.

quiz.prompt: For f(x)=2/(1+x)^3 on x>=0, what is P(X>1)?
quiz.explanation: Integrate using -(1+x)^(-2) from 1 to a finite upper bound b, then let b grow:0-(-1/4)=1/4. The negative sign in the antiderivative is necessary for a positive probability.

flashcards.back: Limit as b -> infinity of the integral from 1 to b; converges if that limit is finite, diverges otherwise.
Integral from 1 to infinity of x^(-p) dx converges iff p > 1; e.g. 1/x^2 -> 1, 1/x diverges.
f >= 0 everywhere and integral over the support equals 1; P(a<=X<=b) = integral from a to b; P(X=x) = 0.
For lambda>0, f(x)=lambda*exp(-lambda*x) on x>=0 and 0 otherwise. For t>=0, survival=exp(-lambda*t); mean=1/lambda and median=ln(2)/lambda.

flashcards.front: Loss density 2/(1+x)^3 on [0, inf): tail probability P(X > 1)?
flashcards.back: 1/4=25%: use antiderivative -(1+x)^(-2), evaluated upper minus lower from 1 to infinity. Density exponent 3 gives survival exponent 2 and infinite second moment.
